summary: Describes the eduroam architecture for federated wireless network access in academia. It combines IEEE 802.1X, EAP and RADIUS so students and staff can sign in at other institutions using home credentials.

plainLanguage.summary: Your school password works at other schools' Wi-Fi around the world, because they all trust each other.

subtitle: Architecture for federated wireless roaming in academic institutions

tldr.problem: Academic institutions want to let students and staff use their home credentials to access Wi-Fi and services at any other participating university worldwide, without each institution maintaining a separate account directory.
tldr.mechanism: eduroam combines IEEE 802.1X port-based authentication, EAP (Extensible Authentication Protocol) for credential transport, and a hierarchical RADIUS proxy fabric to route authentication requests from visiting users back to their home institution for verification.
tldr.outcome: Deployed since 2002 and now serving millions of users across 10,000 service locations on all continents. The architecture has been enhanced with RADIUS/TLS and dynamic discovery to address operational scaling challenges.

today: eduroam remains the primary federated authentication service for academic institutions worldwide. The architecture continues to evolve; RADIUS/TLS is gradually replacing RADIUS/UDP, and dynamic discovery is being deployed in approximately 10 countries. The eduroam PKI, which issues certificates to authorized participants, adds operational complexity but provides strong assurance of peer identity.

sections.title: The Roaming Problem and Solution
sections.content:
In 2002, the European Research and Education community set out to build a network roaming service so students and staff could use their home credentials at any participating institution. Today, eduroam operates at over 10,000 service locations and serves millions of users.

The architecture solves the core problem of trust: a visiting user presents credentials, but the local institution does not have those credentials in its own database. Instead, the local institution trusts a federation of peer institutions and routes the authentication request back to the user's home institution, which verifies the credentials. This approach scales without requiring direct relationships between every pair of institutions.
sections.plainLanguage: When you visit another university's campus and connect to eduroam Wi-Fi, the local access point does not check your password. Instead, it passes your login to your home university, which says yes or no.

sections.title: The Classic Architecture
sections.content:
The architecture rests on three technologies. IEEE 802.1X provides port-based network authentication: when a device connects to a Wi-Fi access point, the access point acts as an authenticator and forwards the access request to an authentication server. EAP (Extensible Authentication Protocol) carries the user's credentials securely inside a TLS tunnel between the user's device and the authentication server, protecting the password even as the request travels through the RADIUS hierarchy.

RADIUS forms the trust fabric: a hierarchy of RADIUS proxy servers at the organizational, national, and global levels routes requests based on the realm part of the user's identity (e.g., surfnet.nl). Each RADIUS server shares a secret with its peers and trusts messages from those peers implicitly. When a request arrives at the user's home RADIUS server (the Identity Provider), that server decapsulates the EAP message and verifies the user credentials.
sections.plainLanguage: The Wi-Fi access point asks your credentials and passes them through a chain of trusted servers until they reach your home school, which knows your password.

sections.title: Operational Problems and Evolution
sections.content:
As eduroam scaled from thousands to millions of authentications, several operational problems emerged. The RADIUS hierarchy initially used UDP, which is unreliable when multiple proxies are on the path: a single lost UDP packet causes a user-visible delay, and firewalls may discard fragmented UDP datagrams carrying large EAP payloads (particularly EAP-TLS with client certificates). Server failures are indistinguishable from downstream failures, leading to false assumptions about which proxy is down.

Routing became complex: realm-based routing works for country-code top-level domains but requires exception entries for realms in generic TLDs like .edu. The static routing table must be manually synchronized across three continents.

Privacy was at risk: RADIUS attributes containing user identity, location information, and device identifiers are sent in cleartext, enabling third parties to track user movements.
sections.plainLanguage: As the network grew huge, it became unreliable. UDP packets got lost, routing got complicated, and attackers could track who was connecting from where.

sections.title: RADIUS/TLS and Dynamic Discovery
sections.content:
In response, eduroam shifted to RADIUS/TLS (RFC 6614), which replaces UDP with TCP and encrypts the entire RADIUS packet payload. TCP ensures that packets arrive in order and rejects fragmentation that firewalls might discard. TLS encryption protects all RADIUS attributes, including privacy-sensitive identity and location data, from IP-layer observers. TLS with X.509 certificates from accredited CAs also authenticates RADIUS peers, replacing the weaker shared-secret model.

Dynamic discovery addresses routing complexity: instead of static configuration, RADIUS servers use DNS NAPTR and SRV records to discover the address of the authentication server for any given realm. The eduroam PKI issues certificates only to authorized participants, and RADIUS servers verify that discovered servers are legitimate eduroam members via OIDs embedded in the certificates.
sections.plainLanguage: The new system uses encrypted connections that cannot be tapped, and servers find each other in DNS instead of using a manual routing table.

sections.title: Security and Privacy Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC discusses multiple threat vectors. Man-in-the-middle attacks are possible if users do not verify EAP server certificates; preconfigured device configurations can mitigate this. Denial-of-service attacks can occur if expired credentials cause cascading authentication failures, and RADIUS servers must manage credential lifetime carefully.

Abuse prevention requires that eduroam participants agree on common policies. When a user violates terms of service, the Service Provider (visited institution) and the Identity Provider (home institution) must coordinate blocking. The protocol includes mechanisms for incident handling through Operator Name attributes and Chargeable User Identity tracking.

Privacy concerns focus on collusion between Service Providers (who see user activity logs) and adversaries. The design encourages anonymous outer identities in EAP and supports pseudonymous client certificates to help users who configure their devices for privacy.
sections.plainLanguage: The network has to protect against fake login servers, credential theft, and tracking. It also needs to allow schools to stop bad actors while respecting student privacy.
